author: AfricanFeminism
title: Laws and Resurgent Cultural Claims: Rwanda’s Decency Policing Erodes Women’s Freedoms
content:
There’s been an online uproar after Rwandan National Police spokesperson ACP Rutikanga Boniface announced on public television that public indecency will be punished. On August 29, police officers threatened to beat young women attending a concert by Tanzanian singer Diamond Platnumz if they did not follow the new ‘decency’ orders.


In Rubavu, a town in the west of the country, a young woman was seen on video being apprehended by police over the length of her dress. Thereafter, several government workers using the X platform stated that it is important for Rwandan culture to be upheld and that the ‘Western ways’ used to sexualize women’s bodies through revealing clothing are corrupting the youth. These are not isolated incidents.


Women’s bodies and the rights of gender-expansive and marginalized people have increasingly become battlegrounds for Christian fundamentalist moralists and lobbyists.


Rwandan law does not clearly define indecency.

Article 143 of Law N° 68/2018 states: “Any person who performs an indecent act in public commits an offence.” Conviction can lead to imprisonment for six months to two years.

 In 2023, there were discussions about redefining indecency as “showing one’s private parts or performing sexual acts in public,” but this was not adopted. Ambiguity remains over what constitute

s a ‘private part,’ making enforcement unclear and subjective. This also opens the door to bias against women and girls, as body parts like shoulders or cleavage may be deemed indecent, similar to theocratic states treating exposed hair as indecent.


Social media is flooded with calls for clarity on the law, as its guidelines would be replicated at entrances to businesses, hotels, and restaurants. This demonstrates how legal ambiguity fuels public scrutiny and the policing of women and girls. Women are speaking up about how legal definitions of decency affect their lives. We cannot live in a world where a mere body can incriminate a person, or where enforcers arbitrarily decide what clothing is

 inappropriate

.


This debate is feeding into an already pervasive culture of gender-based violence whose victims are disproportionately women, girls and gender expansive people. Technology Facilitated Gender Based Violence (TFGBV), already common, is being fueled on TikTok and Instagram, where several young men and some journalists are justifying rape as the woman or girl’s fault due to what she is wearing.


On September 2, a young woman in Kibagabaga was harassed, beaten, undressed, and insulted by a group of men. The video has circulated on social media, but the perpetrators remain unpunished, and the girl’s fate is unknown. Now, online platforms—driven by manosphere communities and technocapitalists profiting from dehumanization—have become battlegrounds for controlling women’s public and private lives.


Mob violence and GBV have been normalized as of late, and public institutions have remained silent. Rwandan women and girls feel ignored, helpless, and abandoned.


The Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion, whose mandate is to champion gender equality, has in the past

 implicitly responded

to rising rates of teenage pregnancies by blaming parents and

mothers for failing to raise ‘decent’ girls

. Once again, the risk in this

rhetoric

is that women, girls, and gender-expansive people become blamed for such deeply rooted systems of inequality and oppression. Subjective matters such as manners, morals, hemline lengths, and even treating nudity as indecency are regressions rooted in colonial and religious control of African bodies.


Counting Women, Not Counting on Rights


All this is happening while women hold 64 percent of seats in parliament, yet they are not fighting against the resurgent social control of women’s bodies or the legal silences that enable it. Rwanda has had a parliamentary women’s majority for nearly two decades, yet this has not resulted in real change, as patriarchal control of women’s lives continues to resurface.


On August 7, 2022, police arrested 24-year-old Liliane Mugabekazi after a photo of her at a concert taken by a journalist circulated online. She was charged with public indecency under Article 143 and faced imprisonment. Prosecutors claimed her clothing “revealed her private parts”—her breasts. A Kicukiro Primary Court judge initially denied her bail. Mugabekazi pleaded not guilty, noting she did not take or share the photo and had passed venue security. She was later …

author: Shams Wang Xin
title: Baptism by the Atlantic: Ethnographic Field Notes on Faith and Renjianshi of Chinese Migration in Cape Verde
content:
Praia, Santiago Island — Jan 1, 2025


[08:32 a.m]


The beach of São Francisco was half-empty when we arrived. The morning light had a metallic edge, slicing through the mist that hung low over the Atlantic. The beach smelled faintly of salt, diesel, and prayer. A speaker played a gospel hymn in Creole, punctuated by waves hitting the rocks.


A small crowd gathered near the shore. Three Chinese men stood apart from the rest, each holding a towel while wearing the pure white cloak. The pastors, two tall Cape Verdean men named João and Manuel, and an invited pastor from South Korea, smiled as they shook their hands. 


[08:50 a.m]


João lifted his Bible, the pages swollen with moisture. “Água é vida,” he said. Water is life. Then he continued, “And life is not divided by language.” That line stayed with me. Around us, Portuguese, Língua Kabuverdianu, Korean, and Mandarin drifted like separate waves, sometimes colliding, sometimes harmonizing.


The three Chinese men listened attentively. The man, Lin Yi, wore a long white cloak that fluttered in the wind. He had come from Wenzhou six months earlier to sell Chinese fried noodles and chicken in Praia’s market. “I didn’t come for baptism,” he told me quietly, “but maybe it came for me.”


[09:10 a.m]


The ceremony began. The pastors waded into the sea, robes soaking, voice steady. “God’s ocean belongs to all,” One of them said. “Today, we return what we are made of.” His voice trembled slightly. The Mandarin phrasing turned the metaphor inward, which is more existential than religious.


[09:20 a.m]


Lin Yi stepped forward. Waves broke around his knees. The water was not that cold, his breath visible. He glanced back once at the shore, not for reassurance, but perhaps to confirm he was really doing this. João raised his hand: “Do you accept the path of faith?” Celina translated, but Lin Yi answered in Creole: “Sim.”


The sea surged, and João forcefully lowered him into the water. For a fleeting moment, the world seemed swallowed by the ocean’s roar. Lin Yi felt the cold seawater instantly envelop him, and in that instant, a fleeting image of the sea back home in Wenzhou, its wind carrying salt and longing, flashed through his mind. When he emerged from the water, the congregation’s song erupted like a tidal wave in his ears, Mandarin hymns intertwining with improvised Creole harmonies, echoing through the sky and sea. There was no expected ecstasy or fear on his face, only a profound calm, a subtle, ineffable smile playing on his lips. It was as if the Atlantic’s depths had washed away all his past, returning a new soul, imbued with the taste of sea salt, completing a silent transformation, a complete farewell to his old self.


[09:40 a.m]


Two Chinese men followed: one from Hebei, one from Wenzhou. Both owned small hardware stores downtown. They laughed nervously as they waded in. Their friends filmed the moment on phones, careful not to drop them in the surf. When it was over, one said in Mandarin, “太咸了。” (“Too salty.”) The congregation applauds. Zhang, one of their friends, films it all on his phone. “Send it home,” he says. “Let them see Africa isn’t just lions. It has blessings too, and these blessings are from the Atlantic.”


[12:00 p.m]


Afterward, we gathered by the beachside for lunch. 


After lunch, the sun had already bathed the beach, and the air was filled with the fragrant char of grilled fish and the salty dampness of the sea breeze, like a silent symphony of flavors. They carefully opened plastic bags, revealing warm pumpkin cakes and soy sauce braised beef, tastes of home. The church members offered golden crispy grilled fish with charred skin, the fresh sweetness of the fish and the tangy zest of lemon wafting forth. Chopsticks and forks gently clinked on plates as people of different skin tones sat in a circle, setting aside words, sharing this simple yet abundant lunch amidst the rhythmic lapping of waves, feeling the primal comfort brought by food, like boats floating on the sea’s surface, each carrying its own stories, but sharing tranquility in the same waters.


João tried to use chopsticks, failed, and laughed until his Bible slipped from his lap. “Faith,” he said, “is learning how to hold new things.” Lin Yi smiled. “Sometimes it’s also about letting go.”


[12:30 p.m]


I asked Lin Yi why he joined the church. He said, “In China, I was too busy to slow down. Here, belief fills the silence.” He paused. “In business, I sell what people …

author: Christopher Rutledge
title: Free speech is not freedom from facts
content:
A strange thing happens to a claim when it moves from a WhatsApp group or a Facebook post into a radio studio. It changes its clothes.


What begins as a rumour on social media can sound very different once it enters a national broadcaster’s studio. The familiar presenter, the recognised station, the rituals of a professional interview, and the authority of being on air all lend the claim credibility it didn’t have before. The listener is no longer hearing merely what someone said online; they are hearing it through an institution they have been taught to trust, and it is easy to assume that if it has reached the microphone, someone must have checked whether it is true.


That is why the recent Broadcasting Complaints Commission of South Africa

(BCCSA) ruling against SAFM

 matters. It is also why some of the criticism of the ruling misses the point.


After SAFM broadcast the apology ordered by the BCCSA, some people asked whether organisations such as Macua (Mining Affected Communities United in Action) were now deciding what could and could not be said in the media. Others suggested that this amounted to controlling the narrative or restricting free speech.


It sounds like a reasonable concern. Nobody should want civil society, government, business or any political organisation to decide which opinions South Africans are permitted to hear.


But that is not what happened here.


We did not ask SAFM to stop interviewing Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, nor did we ask the broadcaster to ban March and March, nor did we ask that controversial views about immigration be removed from the public conversation.


What we were asking was fairly basic: if a claim is presented as fact, particularly on a national broadcaster, the audience is entitled to know what it rests on and whether it can be verified.


The lie about immigrants and crime


Ngobese-Zuma told SAFM listeners that foreign nationals were responsible for 60% of serious crime in Gauteng… Read that sentence again. Not that she believed migrants were contributing to crime. Not that immigration was, in her view, badly managed. She gave a figure: 60%.


A number sounds precise; it sounds researched and official. Once such a number is repeated on national radio, it begins to circulate.


People repeat it at work. Someone forwards it to a WhatsApp family group. A politician quotes it. A Facebook post appears, saying, ‘Even the radio said foreigners commit 60% of crime’.


Soon, nobody remembers where the figure began. They only remember the figure.


However, when the claim was examined, the evidence failed to support it.


GroundUp


and the

Institute for Security Studies

 investigated the broader claims about migrants and serious crime and found no evidence that foreign nationals account for anything approaching such a share of serious crime. Even the prison statistics commonly invoked in these debates do not tell the story people imagine: a significant proportion of foreign nationals in prison are there for immigration-related offences, not the violent crimes usually implied.


And this is the crucial point: saying that a police officer mentioned a figure does not magically make it a reliable statistic, especially since it has been debunked numerous times.


Anti-immigrant, ‘peaceful’ protesters in Alexandra, Johannesburg, carrying weapons and some covering their faces. File photo by Simon Ramapuputla


The BCCSA found that SAFM failed to inquire about the claim’s origins. The commissioner noted that the presenter neither endorsed the 60% claim nor challenged it, leaving listeners to accept it.


That is the distinction between censorship and journalism. Censorship says: you may not say that. Journalism says: you have said it; now show us why we should believe you.


The lie about foreign military bases


The distinction matters because the 60% claim was not the only one. Listeners were also told about foreign military bases allegedly operating in South Africa. They heard allegations that NGOs receiving foreign funding were buying weapons. There were claims that explosives were entering the country and that foreigners were paying police officers.


Again, these are not vague political opinions. Either the military bases exist or they do not. Either particular NGOs are buying weapons or they are not. Either there is evidence of a widespread system in which migrants bribe police officers or there is not.


When

GroundUp

 examined some of these claims, the picture began …

author: Hassan Alnaser
title: 33 Sudanese arrested from Giza public garden face deportation as worsening economic conditions throw many into housing instability
content:
Sudanese businesses operating from Cairo have laid off dozens of workers in recent months as economic conditions worsen in Sudan, according to two informed sources who spoke to Mada Masr and said the layoffs have thrown many Sudanese nationals in the Egyptian capital into housing instability.


The layoffs have forced many to take shelter in public spaces, a situation that Egyptian authorities earlier this week treated as grounds for security intervention.


Some of those laid off from their jobs were among the 33 people whose arrest the Interior Ministry

announced

 in an online statement on Sunday alongside footage of people taking shelter in a public park in 6th of October City in Giza, according to the two sources.


The Interior Ministry stated that security forces acted after the footage circulated online, carrying out an operation that led to the arrests. It added that those detained were not carrying identification documents or residency permits.


All 33 individuals arrested were Sudanese men, and all are currently going through deportation procedures, according to an official at the Sudanese embassy in Cairo, who spoke to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity, as well as the two informed sources: Mohamed Farah and Amgad Taha, both of whom were in contact with some of those arrested.


Farah, who works in Cairo, and Taha, who lives in Aswan and is a relative of one of those detained in the 6th of October City park, each said they know at least five of the men detained on Sunday.


They said the cases are part of a crisis that emerged in July, starting with the loss of jobs, then the loss of housing, which then led people to seek shelter in a public space as a last resort.


The men, many of whom did not have legal documents, were employed by Sudanese companies operating in Egypt that sell goods to markets in Sudan, they said. The men were working in packaging, loading and unloading and similar jobs in return for low wages, and the companies provided food and accommodation, commonly putting about 10 workers in a room, they explained.


As the Sudanese pound has

plummeted

 in value against the dollar in recent months, it has affected operations at the companies, whose Sudan-based revenue streams have been diminished while their costs have remained high.


According to Taha, some of the workers went without pay for as long as three months.


Some businesses shut down or moved their operations back to Sudan, leaving workers with neither their jobs nor their employer-provided housing, Farah and Taha said.


The workers moved in with acquaintances or other workers or tried to look for cheap accommodation, but rising living costs soon made those arrangements unsustainable. Since August, many have resorted to sleeping in public spaces while trying to find another way to support themselves, according to both men.


The Sudanese official at the embassy in Cairo confirmed the situation, adding that some of those turning to public spaces at present are families as well as individual workers.


According to Taha, the cases seen in the parks do not represent the full number of Sudanese people struggling to find housing. Rather, they are the small proportion whose circumstances ended up becoming visible in public spaces.


The detained men, Taha said, are being deported without their complaints being heard, adding that their lack of legal documents had been exploited by their employers.


According to Taha and Farah, many Sudanese young men they know have stayed in Egypt for work while their families returned to Sudan.


The Sudanese embassy official said the embassy handles cases involving Sudanese nationals facing problems with their residency status or being deported through official channels. While declining to comment on the 33 detained people specifically, the official acknowledged that economic conditions have become an important factor in the circumstances of some Sudanese nationals in Egypt.


The war, they added, has led groups of Sudanese people to arrive in Egypt with the intention of finding a temporary refuge. But as the fighting dragged on, their stay has been prolonged, and many have not been able to find stable work while their initial savings have become depleted.


The official stressed the need to distinguish between a legal violation, such as residing in Egypt without the necessary documents — a case they said necessitates deportation — and social circumstances that may put someone in violation of …

author: Signe Marie Cold-Ravnkilde
title: What Europe’s migration deals are really buying
content:
The gravestones are barely visible. Scraps of text scratched into wet cement, left to harden in whatever shape they took. Some have no text at all, just a slight rise in the sand, a low dune along the wall at the far edge of the cemetery in Nouadhibou, Mauritania’s second-largest city and its main Atlantic port, where the Sahara meets the sea. The representative from the municipality walks ahead of us, pointing towards the fringes where the unidentified are buried. Bodies too decomposed to name by the time they reached shore. He has requested a new cemetery, 25km out of town. They are running out of space.

Pirogues on the beach in Nouakchott. Photo by Ahlam Chemlali, March 2026.

We are still standing there when three cars pull up. A battered red Mercedes, followed by two gendarmes in green uniforms who nod at the municipal representative. On an orange stretcher, a white plastic body bag, slightly open. A body has just arrived. The men who came in the cars are from the community — here to try to identify it.

This is what the European Union’s migration partnerships look like from the ground.

Nouadhibou sits on a narrow peninsula on the Atlantic coast, roughly 700km north of the capital Nouakchott, close to the border with Western Sahara and within reach of some of the world’s richest fishing grounds. Since 2006, it has also been the main departure point for migrants attempting the Atlantic crossing to Spain’s Canary Islands. It is this geography — coastal, peripheral, strategically placed — that nakes it the epicenter of the EU’s latest migration partnership.

On March 7, 2024, the European Commission and the Mauritanian government signed a migration deal worth €210 million. The agreement was driven in large part by pressure from Spain, whose interior ministry had recorded a sharp surge in Atlantic arrivals. European officials praised the results. New figures from Frontex, the EU’s border agency, show that detections on the Western African route fell by 63 percent in 2025, driven by sharp drops in departures from Mauritania, Morocco, and Senegal. Spain’s government calls it a success.

We spent two weeks in Mauritania, in Nouakchott and Nouadhibou, interviewing coastguard officials, human rights defenders, municipal representatives, government coordinators, EU and IOM (International Organization for Migration) representatives, fishermen, and migrants. What we found behind the falling numbers tells a different story.

These deals are not simply outsourcing border control. They give states with poor human rights records a mandate, and substantial financing, to do what European governments cannot do at home: detain people without due process, deport them without legal procedure, and sweep entire urban neighborhoods clean of black migrants and refugees in the middle of the night. In exchange, the EU gets the statistics it needs to present the policy as working.

The Tunisia deal, signed on July 16, 2023, was the first iteration of this model. A week later, speaking at a conference in Rome, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was explicit about her intentions:

“

We want our agreement with Tunisia to be a template. A blueprint for the future. For partnerships with other countries in the region.” She has repeated the claim since, including in her State of the Union address that autumn. The EU went on to sign a similar deal with Egypt in March 2024, with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, who came to power in a military coup and has presided over one of the most sweeping crackdowns on civil society in the country’s modern history. Tunisia’s President Kais Saïed, meanwhile, took executive control of the country in July 2021 and has since granted himself unchecked powers to govern and legislate in a rolling power grab. Mauritania is the latest country to be brought into this framework. Understanding what the blueprint produces on the ground, in each of these countries, is not a peripheral concern. It is the point.

In Nouadhibou, that point has a name.

Kamara Mamadou is dressed in a blue shirt, with a striped scarf and a small traditional hat. A retired French teacher, he now helps people navigate a system not designed to receive them — spending years providing legal assistance to detained migrants in Nouadhibou. He is the regional coordinator of AMDH (

Association Mauritanienne des Droits de l’Homme

), Mauritania’s main human rights organization. We meet him on the fifth floor of our hotel, the Atlantic …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Since 2025, Trump Made More Stock Trades Than All 535 Congress Members Combined
content:
This amounts to more than 80 trades per market day for the president in his first 17 months back in office.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

President Donald Trump made nearly 30,000 stock trades since his return to office, marking a far higher volume of trades than all 535 members of Congress combined, a new Bloomberg analysis finds.

Between his inauguration in January 2025 and the end of June, Trump and his team made nearly 28,700 trades, his financial disclosures show. That amounts to roughly 80 trades per market day for nearly a year and a half.

In that period, House lawmakers reported making 19,400 stock trades, while senators reported 2,900, for a total of 22,300 transactions. A few lawmakers were responsible for a large portion of the trades, like Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California), who reported 8,000 transactions in that time.

Trump’s trades have been a major boon for him, as the only modern president who’s ever disclosed trading individual stocks. Previous reports have found that Trump’s 2025 trades alone were worth as much as $1.8 billion, and his trades in the first three months of 2026 were worth as much as $750 million.

These trades have come as he’s driven policy for and outright publicized companies that he has bought stock in; a recent report by Democrats on Congress’s Joint Economic Committee found that Trump has made up to $15.5 million in profits on his oil and gas holdings as the companies’ stocks have risen due to his war on Iran.

Bloomberg also highlights a time when Trump bought as much as $1.4 million in DoorDash stock in the first quarter of 2026, then, in April, staged a stunt where he used DoorDash to deliver McDonald’s to the White House.

The White House has denied accusations of insider trading or improper conduct, saying that his stock portfolio is managed independently and uses a strategy based on computer models. “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” spokesperson Davis Ingle said.

But Trump has also outright opposed any legislation that may prevent him from conducting stock trades — even while he’s backed proposals to bar members of Congress from doing the same.

Last year, Trump attacked Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) for supporting the inclusion of presidents in his bill to ban Congress from trading individual stocks, calling him a “second-tier Senator” and a “pawn” of Democrats.

Even still, during his State of the Union address this year, Trump called for a congressional stock ban to be passed so that members “cannot corruptly profit from using insider information.” Ignoring Trump’s trades, Republicans are using some members’ supposed support of a stock trading ban as a selling point for the party ahead of the midterm elections.

This September, Truthout is celebrating 25 years of publication. For over two decades, we have been a trusted source for fiercely independent journalism thanks to readers like you.

As we look to the next 25 years, we have launched a special fundraising campaign. Looking to a sustainable future for our publication, we have a fundraising goal of $92,000 in the next 8 days.

We are asking for your support at this juncture because we face greater threats than ever before in our organizational history. Trump and his MAGA allies are determined to control the information ecosystem, and movement-based organizations are subject to dangerous censorship and scrutiny.

If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work and our legacy. Anything you can do makes a difference!

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Udlu Hanson named to top 100 most powerful women in Canada
content:
Baffinland Iron Mines Corp.’s vice-president of community and strategic development has been named to the Women’s Executive Network’s 104 most powerful women in Canada.


Udlu Hanson is the first Inuk from Nunavut to receive the honour since 2010, when Kathy Okpik, then the territorial deputy minister of education, was named. 


“That makes me grateful,” Hanson told Nunatsiaq News Wednesday from the Nunavut Trade Show in Iqaluit, where she took part in a panel discussion the day prior.


“That makes me proud to represent the many, many strong Inuit women that have helped impact my career.”


The network released its 24th annual list last week, which celebrates CEOs, entrepreneurs, professionals and leaders in governance and artificial intelligence.


Hanson, who is also the president of the Baffin Regional Chamber of Commerce, has served as an executive at Baffinland for more than seven years. Before that she was a Government of Nunavut deputy minister and CEO of Nunavut Tunngavik Inc.


She said she’s inspired by women who give back to their communities like her mother Ann Hanson, a broadcast journalist and author who served as the third commissioner of Nunavut between 2005 and 2010.


“There’s so many strong Inuit women who belong on that list,” Hanson said. “I think maybe we should have our own.”


Last year, she won a national volunteer achievement award dedicated to recognizing those with 20 years or more of volunteer service. It recognized her role in co-founding the Annauma Community Foundation, a philanthropic organization that provides grant funding to Nunavut-based organizations for projects related to youth, well being, arts and culture, and education.  


She also serves as a director emeritus at the Rideau Hall Foundation and sits on the Governor General’s Reconciliation Advisory Group.


Baffinland congratulated the achievement in a post on social media, noting that her commitment to community transcends far beyond the company.


“This recognition reflects Udlu’s longstanding commitment to advancing Inuit leadership, cultural integration, and community engagement in ways that strengthen long-term, respectful, and mutually beneficial relationships with Inuit communities, Inuit organizations and governments,” the company wrote in a post on Tuesday. 


“Her leadership is embedded in both operational oversight and strategic decision-making, ensuring that Inuit knowledge and priorities are meaningfully reflected in corporate governance and development.”


— With files from Daron Letts

author: Santana Dreaver
title: Call in the goats: Kanaka Bar calls on herd for help with wildfire risk
content:
Wildfire fighting goats are pictured in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


This article has been co-published

with the Narwhal

 as part of their

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship


On a grassy slope in Kanaka Bar, a herd of goats frolic and play. But this isn’t a farm or a petting zoo — it’s an innovative wildfire mitigation effort from the First Nation.


Some of the goats loudly bleat as they chow down on invasive species and overgrown brush. 


A wildfire fighting goat eats vegetation in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


“In the last five years, Kanaka community has been experiencing devastation with fire,” Pauline Michell said.


That includes two evacuations due to wildfires, as well as floods and mudslides that have closed roads and

cut off

 her community from the world. And in Kanaka Bar, there is no fire truck or fire hall.


“Kanaka has solely been on its own in regards to fire,” said Michell. 


Located in Nlaka’pamux territory, twenty kilometers south of Lytton, Kanaka Bar Indian Band also goes by T’eqt’ aqtn’mux, “the crossing place people.” 


A helper greets one of the wildfire fighting goats in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Aaron Hemens/The Narwhal


In 2021, the Lytton Creek wildfire devastated the area, evacuating numerous First Nations for years at a time, while burning structures and homes to the ground. 


Later that year, an

atmospheric river

 raged through the Fraser and Thompson Rivers, washing out roads and cutting people off from leaving Kanaka Bar.


According to a

new report from the office of the B.C. Human Rights Commissioner

, between 2000 and 2024, First Nation reserves accounted for 36 of 37 communities where at least half of the total land area was burned by wildfire, with the only non-reserve community being Lytton.


Vegetation that had been previously grazed by wildfire fighting goats, near the entrance to Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


Further, First Nation reserves in “B.C.” are four times more likely to be impacted by wildfire than non-reserve communities. 


This prompted Michell, an elected councillor in her community, to take a proactive approach to the wildfire season. 


For eight weeks starting in late July, a herd of goats ate their way through the Kanaka Bar Indian Band, targeting areas with built up fuel and brush that would burn up in a fire. 


A wildfire fighting goat eats vegetation in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


About 80 goats have been clocking in this summer, while a few goats — like Dandelion and Cuddley — are part of a rebel club in their own separate enclosure.


“This is a trial for Kanaka, to look at fuel management in this way,” said Michell. 


“Hearing about these goats being able to do this sounded really intriguing and interesting, they’ve been here for about a month now.”


Wildfire fighting goats are pictured in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


The idea came by accident, after an area grazed by sheep acted as a fire stop during a wildfire three years prior. 


“Back in 2023, the Kookipi Creek fire came through … we had been grazing the sheep that we had out in this back area, and when that fire came through, it actually came pretty much all the way down to community, and then it stopped where the sheep had been grazing,” Emma Bryce said.


She recalled thinking, “This is really cool, we just kind of made our own fire break without really intending to.”


Emma Bryce, the lead for a project of goats fighting wildfires, is pictured with the goats in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


Bryce has been the nation’s food self-sufficiency lead since 2022, and after the sheep experience, started researching different animals to graze in the community. 


“In conversations with chief and council, I brought it up and was like, ‘What if we used goats to do wildfire risk reduction?’ They were like, ‘okay, let’s do it,'” she said.


“This goat grazing project has been a passion project of mine for the last couple of years,” Bryce added, after she took the green light from Kanaka and ran with it. That’s when she met Bruce Bradley, who does contract work across “B.C.” with his herd of goats. 


Bruce Bradley of BC Timber Goats holds one of his baby goats in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


Based on “Vancouver Island,” it took three trips by ferry to bring his …

author: Sara Connors
title: Couple on quest to learn more about 19th century bentwood box
content:
As soon as Tlingit artist Joanne Williams laid eyes on the bentwood box she and husband Maurice would eventually travel over 4,800 kilometres round trip to retrieve, she knew it was meant to be.


“As soon as I saw it, I had to take a big breath and realise that I’m going to go get this box no matter what it takes us,” she told

APTN News.


The pair recently acquired a bentwood box from a private seller in Washington state that they believe dates back to the 19th century and whose design suggests it may be of Tlingit origin.


Typically made from a single sheet of bent cedar, bentwood boxes were historically used for both practical and ceremonial purposes. They stored everything from food to regalia to canoe tackle and also served as important items in burials and funerals.


The Williamses, who are

bentwood box knowledge-holders and teachers

 based in Atlin, British Columbia, said the box is a remarkable find as those dating back to the 19

th

 century or earlier are generally only found in museums.


“It’s a fluke of luck,” Williams said. “This is a gift from the ancestors. It’s the only way it could be found.”


Williams said the seller, who lives near Blaine, Washington, inherited the box from his grandmother, a private collector who lived in Ketchikan, Alaska.


According to her, around 300 people were interested in buying the box, with offers reaching as high as $60,000 USD.


Williams said her work with bentwood boxes helped her stand out from the other buyers, and that the seller ultimately chose her as it was his grandmother’s wish to reunite cultural items in her collection with their rightful communities.


“As soon as the seller got a hold of me and told me that he made his mind up that only I would be getting it, I was sure that my ancestors were guiding me and making this happen for us,” she said.


The Williamses purchased the box with their own funds for $10,000 USD.


The box features U-shaped ovoids, or formline design. Photo: Submitted


The pair travelled from their home in Atlin to Washington state earlier this summer, braving intense wildfires to retrieve the sacred item. Williams said the trip was further complicated by

new U.S. rules on shipping art across the border

 and a days-long delay by her bank in releasing the funds needed for the purchase.


But she said the journey was well worth it when she first saw the item.


“I had tears in my eyes. I was overwhelmed with the feeling that my ancestors were right near me,” she said.


Williams acknowledged she’s received some criticism for buying the item from a seller, but argued it’s sometimes necessary to ensure cultural items return to their rightful communities.


“That’s one of the biggest things that people were complaining about,” she said. “(But) if I didn’t do it, I wouldn’t have it in my hands right now. I would have missed out.”


The purchase is reminiscent of another sacred item involving Williams’ First Nation, the Taku River Tlingit.


The band paid an auction house around $40,000 in 2022 for a

19

th

 century Chilkat robe

, which has since been

returned to the community

.


Not much known about box—at least not yet


Williams said formline imagery on the box indicates it might, in fact, originate from her own First Nation. She said she is not sharing what those images are for the time being because many people have contacted her claiming the box comes from their community.


The Williams’ are safekeeping the box at Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia (UBC) while non-invasive work is conducted to find out more about its origins.


That work will include analysing the paint used and also inviting other bentwood box makers to examine it.


Sue Rowley, the museum’s director, agrees that the box has characteristics of Tlingit design.


She said clues suggesting its origin include the ovoids it features—elongated circles with flattened bottoms typical of Tlingit formline design. She also noted the box appears to be painted with both burnt, ground-up bone and red ochre, and that operculum, or sea snail shells, were used on the lid—materials commonly found in Tlingit communities.


“What a stunning example this is of incredible craftsmanship, artwork, art history, and cultural significance of bentwood boxes on the Northwest Coast, and looking (very much like) bentwood boxes of the 19th century,” she said.


Maurice said the advanced craftsmanship required to make the box makes it even more remarkable …

author: Bianca Blell
title: Record ICE Arrests Reveal the Expanding Reach of Immigration Enforcement
content:
In June of 2026, US immigration officers, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), arrested a record of 43,138 people. The figure represents the highest number of arrests since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025 and an increase of 5,450 people from early April, an almost 15% difference. The increase comes as immigration enforcement operations have expanded across the country.

This three-month gap in data raises concerns about transparency. Since 2019, Congress has required ICE to publish data on arrests, detentions, and deportations every two weeks. However, the agency did not publish updated figures between early April and July. ICE attributed the delay to a series of government shutdowns.

As of July 11, 65,765 immigrants were detained at detention centers across the country, compared with a record of 70,700 people in January. Since Trump was sworn in this term, over 610,000 immigrants have been detained. The latest figures show that people without a criminal history continue to make up a larger share of those detained than people with pending charges or criminal convictions.

A recent increase in funding towards Border Patrol and Customs agencies occurred in June, the same month the arrest record was at its highest. This $70 billion bill passed by the US Senate on June 5th and the House on the 9th surged ICE’s monetary resources, a budget which will extend into 2029, past the current administration.

The expanded funding passed amid sharp disagreement in Congress. Republican lawmakers argued that the funding was necessary to support ICE and Border Patrol, while Democratic lawmakers raised concerns about the administration’s immigration enforcement tactics. Those concerns included the federal response in Minneapolis, where ICE officers fatally shot US citizens Renée Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in January.

Pretti’s passing transpired during Minneapolis protests opposing Good’s killing and the treatment of immigrants in the community. ICE agents targeting vulnerable populations in a city grieving for one of their residents points to concerns of violations against citizens’ First Amendment rights to protest.

Following the Minneapolis operations, the administration began shifting away from the highly visible raids that had characterized some of its earlier immigration operations. After Kristi Noem was replaced as secretary of Homeland Security by Markwayne Mullin in March 2026, immigration enforcement increasingly moved toward smaller, more targeted operations. These include targeted attacks at hospitals, schools, outside homes, during traffic stops, and at mandatory immigration check-in appointments.

The administration has also set ambitious arrest targets. In May 2025, the Trump administration reportedly stated a quota goal of 3,000 immigration arrests per day.

The scale of immigration enforcement is also raising concerns about the treatment of people during arrest and detention. The ACLU documented more than 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents. This violence includes killing citizens and immigrants, causing bodily harm which could result in death, and destroying property all while masked and many times in front of young children.

The record number of arrests reflects a broader expansion of immigration enforcement. The expansion raises questions about the state of American democracy and the checks and balances intended to protect individual rights. These protections cannot depend on a person’s immigration status.

author: Admin100
title: One Million Hands Flourishing: Nicaragua and the Neverending Task of Planting
content:
By Tamaya F.C.


The indigenous neighborhood of Monimbo in Masaya, Nicaragua has a long legacy of resistance. Masaya is located less than an hour Southeast of the capital, Managua. In 1978, the people of Monimbo barricaded themselves, used makeshift weapons and prevented the National Guard from coming into the city, winning the first major victory for the Sandinistas as they were able to take control of an urban city. Forty years later, the people of Monimbo barricaded themselves with paving stones and were able to prevent riot police from entering. The next day however, they had lost most of the city to riot police. Masaya, the city where I am from, has become a battlefield where police attack citizens.


The Unrest


The latest civil unrest has had many university students from across the capital city of Managua protesting against the government’s social security reforms this past week. These students hail from various universities like the Universidad Centroamericana (UCA), Universidad Nacional de Ingenieria (UNI), Universidad Nacional Agraria (UNA), Universidad Autónoma Nacional de Nicaragua – Managua (UNAN)

,

and Universidad Politécnica de Nicaragua (UPOLI). The  proposal was to increase social security contribution from both workers and employers and

reduce retiree benefits

 by 5%.


Last week, students barricaded the Metropolitan Cathedral in Managua which serves as a refuge for protesters. There, they collected donations and distributed provisions such as water and had student doctors help tend to the wounded. Police and pro-government Sandinista youth eventually surrounded the cathedral and held them hostage until prominent Catholic church official, Monsignor Silvio Jóse Báez, who has been critical of Ortega and supportive of protesters, aided and helped assure the release of the students.


Sandinista Legacy


When the Sandinistas (FSLN) overthrew the Somoza regime in July 1979, they had to work toward reconstructing the social, political and economic structure of the country. They implemented

agrarian reforms

 for redistribution of land, launched

 vaccination campaigns

 to open access to healthcare and created

literacy campaigns

 that reduced illiteracy from 80 percent to 12 percent, among other reforms. This was only possible because of the work everyday people put in day after day.


Over the last five days, more than 30 people have died, many of them students as well as a journalist. Over 100 are being held prisoner, around 50 remain missing and the overall count of those injured is unknown.


On April 22nd, Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, who rose to power as a prominent leader of the Sandinistas, revoked the proposed changes to social security. After he pulled the reforms, riot police entered a prominent symbol of the student resistance, UPOLI, which students had barricaded. Five students were shot in the process and two were killed. Ortega also attacked the student movement as “delinquents” who were backed by right-wing parties and funded by the CIA. The student movement does not allow

political parties to participate

 though. But many Nicaraguans know this is an issue greater than social security. They are tired of corrupt governments and want the current government out.


I am an anarchist. So w

hen I say “I am a Sandinista” to me it means I believe in the popular movement that rose up to overthrow capitalist imperialism. The movement that fought for freedom. The movement that dared to dream of bringing a just and equitable society.


The current government of Ortega does not represent the values of Sandino nor of the Sandinistas who spilled blood to break free from their chains in previous decades. The Sandinista Youth of today is not the same one that my mother joined many years ago. It is not the one that participated in literacy campaigns to teach the people to read and write, nor is it the one she joined to help pick coffee and rebuild Nicaragua.


The Demands of the Students


The future is uncertain and it is unclear where this is all heading but there is much work to be done on the ground. Today, students from the

Movimiento 19 de Abril

, who embody the spirit of liberation are undertaking the never ending task of building a new world, one from the bottom up. Approximately 500 students continue their barricaded occupation of UPOLI and their organizing against Ortega. They are currently working on establishing a coordinating body to represent students from different …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Sarah Paulson Will Play Six Characters in ‘American Horror Story: 13’
content:
American Horror Story: 13 is set to be quite the clusterfuck. Whether that’s a good thing or a bad thing…only time will tell.

It’s hard to believe, but the cultural phenomenon of American Horror Story started 15 years ago with the season retroactively called Murder House. It was groundbreaking and scary and dramatic and unlike most things we had seen on TV before. Its success launched a franchise that has attracted wide audiences and a truly bonkers array of celebrity guest stars, from Kim Kardashian to Angela Bassett to Patti LuPone. The show has also seen plenty of LGBTQ+ actors come through its ranks, including but definitely not limited to Lady Gaga, Cara Delevingne, Angelica Ross, and of course, Sarah Paulson, who has been in 10 of the show’s 13 seasons, including this upcoming one.

In fact, a lot of actors from previous seasons will be reprising their roles for Season 13, with Sarah Paulson playing SIX of her characters. Jessica Lange will return as some combination of the four character she has played throughout the series, Ryan Murphy having pulled her back in despite explicitly stating she wasn’t going to return to the series. Plus, some new faces will show up; for example, Tig Notaro!

It does seem like, from the trailer, they’re pulling from the early days of AHS, aka truly the best seasons. I personally watched and enjoyed Murder House, Asylum, Coven, and Hotel, but had to quit Freak Show, Roanoke, and Apocalypse before they were over. I stopped 1984 after one episode because Will Schuster was in short shorts and it hurt my eyes. I never even attempted Double Feature, NYC, or Delicate. I watched but did not particularly enjoy the anthology spinoff, American Horror Stories. So I’m torn about this, if I’m honest. On one hand, Coven was my second favorite season and the trailer has the titular coven reassembling, which could be epic. On the other hand, it’s Ryan Murphy. And you never really know what you’re going to get with him. So, I hope that this is either surprisingly amazing, or at least so bad it’s fun to watch. I feel like you can’t REALLY go wrong with Sarah Paulson Tatiana Maslany-ing all over the place, but there’s only one way to find out.

If you also aren’t fully up to date on your AHS lore but don’t have time for any full-season rewatches, the official account has provided a handy dandy rewatch list of 13 episodes to prepare you for AHS: 13.

You can check out the trailer now, and the first episode will air on September 24th. It will take us right into spooky season, with the finale airing the Thursday before Halloween.

author: Unknown
title: A New Issue of Inside Front : For Anarcho-Punks and Hardcore Anarchists
content:
Over three decades ago, some of the first people to collaborate on CrimethInc. projects met via the international networks that had developed in the zine underground associated with the

hardcore punk scene

. One of the first projects they collaborated on was the hardcore zine

Inside Front

, the archives of which are available

here

.


In those days, without the internet, how did people discover and pass on anarchist ideas and tactics?


By embedding these values in rebellious subcultural milieus such as the punk scene—by reading dogeared books about the Yippies, the Situationists, and the Spanish Civil War—and by having adventures.


These three elements—subculture, reading, and adventure—came together in the hardcore journal Inside Front.


The

last issue

 of

Inside Front

 came out in 2003.


In August 2025, as the hardcore band

Catharsis

 was preparing to play their first shows debuting their album “

Hope against Hope

,” the team behind

Inside Front

 suddenly came out of retirement and threw together a new issue of the magazine in a week flat.


As a consequences of some wrongheaded notions about authenticity and immediatism, the issue never appeared online, though Catharsis distributed them from New York City to Budapest.


Never, at least, until now.


We’ve added this

new issue of

Inside Front

 to our online archive, so you can print and distribute your own copies.


From the introduction:


We hastily prepared this special limited edition of Inside Front in just a few days, scrambling to finish it in time for the record release shows for the Catharsis LP “Hope against Hope.” Although it has been well over two
decades since the previous issue, many people who contributed to previous issues of Inside Front sent new material for this one—not to mention at least one contributor who was not yet born when the first issues of

Inside Front

 appeared.


Copies of the new issue of

Inside Front

 on a literature table in Budapest. This is like sighting a coelacanth in the wild.


From a

review

 by Martin on the

Counterforce

 site:


The cover says “For anarcho-punks and hardcore anarchists” and I could just stop the review right there. This might be the epitome of “perfect zine” for me. The first non-meta content is “Like Weeds – A Dialogue about HIS HERO IS GONE’s Timeless Anthem” in which two thinkers trade increasingly deep and heady observations and anecdotes about the song and it’s context (even more impressive when you realize both parties are almost certainly completely sober).


There’s also a relatable story about en EXTREME NOISE TERROR CD triggering scrutiny at the US border, a show review from someone’s first hardcore show ever, top-10 lists, a few reviews, ideas for a Stateless Fair, and a pair of parallel accounts from fighters in the Syrian civil war bonding over a Czechoslovakian hardcore song they all happened to know, and the struggle to finally download and listen to the song in the middle of a war zone.


It feels like a special and unique zine, since it draws on energy built up over 20+ years since the last issue. I’m not sure if Inside Front will return in a more permanent way, but I hope this issue gets wider distribution than just the CATHARSIS tour so more of you can enjoy it.


From the introduction to the zine:


Why hardcore, still, today, in the year 2025?


In the 1990s, in a time of social peace (at least in the United States), the hardcore scene was ahead of the times in that it was hyper-connected, internationally networked, and artistically experimental.


Today, the hardcore scene is increasingly conservative, artistically speaking (though we challenge you to prove us wrong!). It’s no longer any better networked than any other social milieu. But it is now old-fashioned in a potentially explosive way, because it involves physical collectivity, togetherness that unfolds on a slower time frame than the virtual reality of internet relations.


People have also become more aesthetically literate than they used to be. Whereas both a blast beat and a black bloc were completely foreign and incomprehensible to most people in 1999 (and both models derived both their strength and their limits from that fact), today, a much wider range of people can understand both of them. Yet as these reference points have become more widely shared, a crucial detail of the punk program has been lost: context is everything.

author: C4SS
title: Attacco alla Libertà Tecnologica e al Dissenso
content:
C4SS

. Pubblicato l’otto settembre 2026 con il titolo

An Attack on Tech Freedom, an Assault on Dissent

. Traduzione di

Enrico Sanna

.


Viviamo in un mondo caratterizzato da

stato di polizia

,

militarizzazione della polizia

, e

repressione


del


dissenso

. Con i colossi aziendali spesso alleati con lo stato per

mettere a tacere chi dissente

 o per rafforzare la

sorveglianza

.


Dato il contesto, è importante che i gruppi autonomi abbiano piattaforme di comunicazione e hosting criptate.


Per aver fatto ciò, un collettivo italiano è stato recentemente

dichiarato

 “associazione terroristica globale” dall’amministrazione Trump. Il collettivo è Autistici/Inventati, che offre servizi ad attivisti tramite il servizio di hosting

NoBlogs

 e altre infrastrutture digitali.


Secondo

 il dipartimento di stato degli Stati Uniti, “Autistici/Inventati (A/I) è un gruppo estremista con base in Italia che crea e gestisce infrastrutture digitali al servizio di cellule antifasciste (antifa) violente e gruppi militanti di estrema sinistra in tutto il mondo”.


L’accento sulle

cellule antifasciste

 riflette il tentativo in corso dell’amministrazione Trump di abbattere il dissenso demonizzando gli “antifascisti”. Questo è l’obiettivo esplicito del memorandum presidenziale sulla sicurezza nazionale (

NSPM-7

), ed è alla base delle azioni penali contro gli attivisti anti-CIE (che gestisce i rimpatri), come

Minneapolis 15

 e

Prairieland defendants

.


Nel loro desiderio ossessivo di collegare tutto il dissenso anarchico e di sinistra agli “antifascisti”, l’amministrazione Trump è incorsa in dichiarazioni sfacciatamente false. Così il dipartimento di stato:


L’organizzazione antifascista Rose City, con base nell’Oregon, si è servita di strutture e servizi del collettivo A/I per coordinare e spingere a compiere localmente atti violenti e criminali, compreso un attacco contro gli elicotteri della polizia di frontiera che ha portato ad una denuncia federale. Rose City si è inoltre servita di strumenti e servizi di A/I per diffondere liste di proscrizione e informazioni personali ottenute illegalmente sulla polizia di frontiera, oltre a inviti a prendere di mira agenti in strada e “in casa loro”.


Ma come

fa notare

 la rete antifascista Torch, Rose City non è responsabile di tali azioni e non si serve di A/I. Gli agenti federali si riferiscono ai comunicati di Rose City Counter-Info, un’organizzazione completamente diversa che fa uso dei servizi di A/I. “Rose City” è un appellativo molto comune a Portland, nell’Oregon. Il nome accomuna organizzazioni diverse tra loro. Si tratta di chiare falsità ingenuamente amplificate da giornalisti di

Fox News

 e

National Review

.


Al di là dell’incompetenza dimostrata, dire che il collettivo A/I è una “associazione terroristica globale” è, questa sì, una minaccia serissima. Come

afferma

 il coordinatore tecnico di C4SS William Gillis, “È un FORTE attacco contro il diritto elementare di libertà di parola. Non oso immaginare quale colpo potrebbe subire un movimento anarchico costituito, come dicono gli Stati Uniti, da 5.500 mailing list e 10.000 blog.”


Il dipartimento di stato punta il dito contro gli utenti dei servizi di A/I accusandoli di aver commesso presunti reati, come il sabotaggio e il terrorismo. Ma si tratta perlopiù di attività che rientrano chiaramente nel primo emendamento (libertà di parola, religione, stampa e assemblea,

NdT

). Ci rientrano l’organizzazione di fiere del libro anarchico, attività di ricerca antifascista che studiano e denunciano organizzazioni di estrema destra e anche il blog di una rivista accademica di revisione paritaria e una trasmissione radio con podcast anarchico.


Classificare A/I come “associazione terroristica globale” significa a sanzioni. Significa che chiunque faccia transazioni con A/I si espone a rappresaglie legali, e questo sulla base di un decreto dell’esecutivo. Il risultato è che il sito del collettivo è stato

chiuso

,

PayPal

 ha bloccato il conto e lo stesso conta di fare l’italiana

Banca Etica

,


Si tratta di sanzioni che hanno un effetto devastante per A/I.

Così


Sabot Media

: “Il sei settembre, undici giorni dopo che gli Stati Uniti hanno messo il collettivo italiano nell’elenco delle attività terroristiche, A/I ha annunciato che chiuderà, tutti i servizi di email, blogging, hosting e comunicazioni offerti da venticinque anni saranno interrotti.”


Un precedente agghiacciante. Il governo può …

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: War-Damaged Building in Gaza Collapses, Killing 21, as Gaza Remains Unlivable
content:
Two thousand buildings damaged by Israeli bombing are currently sheltering people across Gaza.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In the early hours of Wednesday morning, a building damaged by Israeli strikes collapsed in Gaza, killing at least 21 people, including 11 children.

An estimated 100 people were living in the six-story building when it collapsed as residents were sleeping. Rescue teams worked to pull out dozens of people from the rubble in the hours that followed, their work made more difficult due to the lack of much-needed equipment.

Wednesday’s collapse is a reminder of the unliveable conditions in Gaza, in particular the lack of safe housing and absence of a rebuilding process amid Israel’s genocide. Though the collapsed building had previously been damaged by Israeli bombing, displaced families had moved in due to the lack of available options for shelter.

Gaza’s Civil Defense warned that 2,000 damaged buildings are currently sheltering people across Gaza, in unsafe conditions, due to a lack of safe alternatives.

“The building collapse in Gaza should be enough of a wake-up call for the international community to pressure Israel to allow reconstruction materials and caravans into Gaza,” Euro-Med Monitor stated on X. “Displaced Palestinians need safe places to live, and they need them now.”

Since the start of the genocide, approximately 1.9 million Palestinians in Gaza, or around 90 percent of Gaza’s population, have been displaced – many of them multiple times.

In August, the United Nations stated that approximately 82 percent of structures in Gaza – about 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with two thirds of them completely destroyed. They added that the destruction of buildings has increased by nearly 10 percent since the so-called ceasefire began in October 2025. Since then, global attention and pressure on Israel has waned, even as the genocide has continued and conditions of life in Gaza have further deteriorated.

Since 2023, Israel has imposed a near-total blockade on the entry of heavy machinery needed to clear wreckage and rescue people trapped under buildings Israel has bombed. As a result, the Palestinian Civil Defense has estimated that there are over 8,000 people who remain unrecovered from destroyed buildings. Despite the so-called ceasefire in October 2025, Israeli officials have still refused to allow the entry of necessary rescue equipment.

No reconstruction work has taken place in Gaza. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace has conditioned rebuilding and reconstruction on the disarmament of Hamas – which Hamas agreed to in July, on the condition that Israel halts its attacks on Gaza.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration approved one of the largest military aid packages to Israel on Tuesday, a $2.8 billion sale of heavy weapons including 20,000 BLU-117 bombs, 20,000 MK-84 bombs, and 20,000 bunker-busting I-2000 warheads – heavy munitions that are designed to destroy buildings and that have left thousands of deep craters across Gaza.

This September, Truthout is celebrating 25 years of publication. For over two decades, we have been a trusted source for fiercely independent journalism thanks to readers like you.

As we look to the next 25 years, we have launched a special fundraising campaign. Looking to a sustainable future for our publication, we have a fundraising goal of $92,000 in the next 8 days.

We are asking for your support at this juncture because we face greater threats than ever before in our organizational history. Trump and his MAGA allies are determined to control the information ecosystem, and movement-based organizations are subject to dangerous censorship and scrutiny.

If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work and our legacy. Anything you can do makes a difference!

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Nunavik police identify suspects in fires across 3 communities
content:
Nunavik police say they have identified suspects in a string of recent fires across Puvirnituq, Akulivik and Kuujjuaq.


Speaking Monday at the Kativik Regional Government council meeting in Inukjuak, Chief Jean-François Bernier said police arrested one person last weekend and that several suspects are children aged 12 and under.


The investigation covers incidents that occurred over several months. Investigators have ruled out that on serial adult arsonist could be behind the fires, said police public relations manager Julie Berthold in an email Wednesday.


Nunatsiaq News asked Berthold for a timeline and details of the fires that are being investigated but she declined to provide more information, citing the active investigation.


Many of the properties targeted are abandoned or unoccupied houses and shacks, Bernier told councillors during Monday’s meeting. He urged people in the affected communities to report sightings of anybody they see around these buildings at night.


“What I’m asking is that people call us immediately so that we send the patrol on the spot to catch them,” Bernier said.


Bernier said police have increased patrols in Puvirnituq, the most affected community, while investigators review what the chief described as hundreds of pieces of video evidence.


Officers are also asking people to submit information or video through the Nunavut Police Service’s confidential tip line (tips@nunavikpolice.ca) or directly with a police officer.


The police service has not released further details about the suspects or the circumstances surrounding the incidents.

author: Zoë Yunker
title: Chinook are going blind on the Salmon River amid worsening drought conditions
content:
Over the summer, the Salmon River has slowed to a trickle, leaving fish in trouble in its warming waters. Photo courtesy of Secwépemc Fisheries Commission


This story originally appeared


in The Tyee


here

 and is reprinted with permission and minor style edits

.

It includes a photo of a Chinook salmon in distress that may be unsettling

 —

please look after your spirit and read with care.


In the Shuswap, Chinook salmon circle a small pool, preparing for the next leg of their journey up the Salmon River to spawn.


But this year, something is different: the salmon’s eyes have gone cloudy; some have fallen out entirely. The river they depend on has caused them to go blind.


For salmon, living conditions in the river are among the worst they’ve ever been. What was once a wide, cool waterway is now a thin, warm channel. Water can become a death trap, causing the fish to suffocate and sometimes lose vision. Blinded salmon are unlikely to live long enough to spawn.


In July, the province 

issued

 a protection order to limit irrigation throughout the region in the hope of reducing the destruction now underway. The order was 

rescinded

 less than two weeks later, with officials citing the interests of industrial water users intent on irrigating their crops as wildfires loomed. The order was then 

reissued

 on Aug. 19, after hundreds of chinook had arrived in the watershed.


Whether this year’s returning salmon will survive remains unclear.


Winding its way from the plateaus west of Okanagan Lake northeast to Shuswap Lake, the Salmon River is surrounded by intensive water users, including large ranches and farms. In recent years historically low levels of snowpack and precipitation have compounded those pressures, leading to unprecedented levels of water scarcity.


In the Salmon River, chinook salmon have gone blind over the summer because of deteriorating water conditions. Photo courtesy of Secwépemc Fisheries Commission


Orders restricting access to the Salmon River’s water have become an almost yearly occurrence as the region faces consecutive years of extreme drought. But this year’s first order came with an ominous distinction: stream flows were far lower than in any year previous, and the order came weeks earlier into the dry season.


Encoded in “B.C.’s” system of water laws, an emergency order is meant to be a last-ditch lever that authorities can pull when fish survival is at imminent risk. But in several watersheds they are now being used on a regular basis as the province faces ongoing drought.


Rosie Simms, director of place-based projects at the POLIS Water Sustainability Project at the University of Victoria, said the repeated use of orders is a sign that things need to change.


“We can’t be trying to fix drought in an emergency,” Simms said. She recently co-authored a 

report

 that documented patterns of prolonged drought across the province and called for a preventive approach to managing water in an era of increasing water scarcity.


“There’s a whole suite of things that would set us British Columbian communities up to be in a much better place to weather droughts and actually live well in drier conditions.”


In an email, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship wrote that “government has made preparing for drought conditions and responding to water scarcity a top priority, to safeguard the well-being of communities, businesses, ecosystems and wildlife.” They added that “the province is also working with partners on long-term, proactive solutions to improve water security in drought-prone watersheds.”


The water crisis in the southern Interior was anticipated long before the chinook began their journey upstream. In May, the Okanagan Nation Alliance 

declared

 a “watershed emergency” across rivers throughout the region, including the Salmon and Bessette watersheds.


The alliance of six Okanagan First Nations called for actions such as mandatory reductions in water use to protect fish flows and a co-governance forum between the syilx and the province to address water scarcity.


“Water is life, and the health of our watersheds can no longer be treated as secondary to development and short-term interests,” Westbank First Nation Chief Robert Louie said in a press release at the time.
